Reconstructing faces from DNA

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scientists can now reconstruct a face of a person if they have DNA only

Summary:
The face of a killer constructed from DNA left at the scene of a crime: it sounds like science fiction. But revealing the face of a criminal based on only their genes may be closer than we think. Today scientists are using genetic markers from DNA to build up a picture of a person with some degree of accuracy.

Further information:
BUILDING THE FACE OF A CRIMINAL FROM DNA
The face of a killer constructed from DNA left at the scene of a crime: it sounds like science fiction. But revealing the face of a criminal based on their genes may be closer than we think.
Today scientists are using genetic markers from DNA to build up a picture of an offender's face, a process known as molecular photo fitting.
A DNA profile is only useful to detectives if a match can be found on a database. This technology offers the tantalising prospect of generating a face from nothing more than a few cells. Dr Peter Claes, a medical imaging specialist at the University of Leuven is doing exactly this.
Along with colleagues in the US, he's built up a database of faces and DNA. And armed with this information, he's able to model how a face is constructed based on just 20 genes.
Dr Claes believes it contains a lot of information that would be useful to detectives: "I can tell you that your eyebrows are sticking forward more, and your chin as well," he explains.
"You have a very prominent specific chin compared to an average European, which in my eyes is not a bad result. You do tend to have flat cheeks, but of course that's a tricky area to actually predict accurately because it's heavily based on diet, which is an environmental factor."
At the moment, police couldn't publish a molecular photo-fit like this and hope to catch a killer. But that's not how Dr Claes sees the technique being used in a criminal investigation.
"If I were to bring this result to an investigator, I wouldn't necessarily give him the image to broadcast. I would talk to him and say okay, you're looking for a woman, with a very specific chin and eyebrow structure.
"So if you're having suspects or candidates that you're looking for, just focus on those."
This may be new science, but Dr Claes and his colleagues are rapidly developing the technology.
The number of genes used is being expanded from 20 to 200, and is seems clear that molecular photo-fitting is only going to become extremely accurate in the coming years.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SCIENTISTS RECONSTRUCT FACES FROM DNA SAMPLES
Sometime in the future, technicians will go over the scene of the crime. They’ll uncover some DNA evidence and take it to the lab. And when the cops need to get a picture of the suspect, they won’t have to ask eyewitnesses to give descriptions to a sketch artist – they’ll just ask the technicians to get a mugshot from the DNA.
That, at least, is the potential of new research being published today in PLOS Genetics. In that paper, a team of scientists describe how they were able to produce crude 3D models of faces extrapolated from a person’s DNA.
“We show that facial variation with regard to sex, ancestry, and genes can be systematically studied with our methods, allowing us to lay the foundation for predictive modeling of faces,” the researchers wrote in their paper. “Such predictive modeling could be forensically useful; for example, DNA left at crime scenes could be tested and faces predicted in order to help to narrow the pool of potential suspects.”
To arrive at their facial reconstructions from DNA, the researchers looked at the genes that seem to correlate with facial structures, the facial structures of the people with those genes, and then asked people outside of their research group to characterize facial structures along different axes. All of these factors were then used to develop statistical models to approximate a facial structure from DNA.
Of course, the process at this point is far from perfect, and there are plenty of obstacles in the way. This study is only for a limited set of genes and populations, and of course, there are many other factors that go into what a face looks like beyond mere genes, such as age and weight.
As the researchers note in the paper, “much more work is needed before we can know how many genes will be required to estimate the shape of a face in some useful way and many more populations need to be studied before we can know how generalizable the results are.” Still, they add, “these results provide both the impetus and analytical framework for these studies.”
Which means that until it is shown that there is a general way to reconstruct faces from DNA (and it may turn out that there isn’t), cops will still have to find suspects in old-fashioned ways. But if this research pans out, it will provide one more tool that law enforcement can use to accurately determine who might have committed a crime.

Press Release:


Building the Face of a Criminal
Astonishing advances in genetics are boosting the war on crime. Scientists are able to reconstruct faces from DNA traces left at crime scenes, revealing what a perpetrator may look like well before police have identified him. Carte Blanche explores the technology that is set to change the face of criminal investigations.


Script:


V/O:
These images are versions of the faces of living individuals and for the most part, they are quite accurate.
Devi:
And what makes them really special is the fact that the man who created these images has never met anyone of these people, nor has he seen photographs of them.
V/O:
He only had some saliva containing their DNA.

And using just the DNA, he created the images of them and others. It sounds unbelievable, but it is not as far-fetched as it seems.

Shaped as a twisted double helix and present in every cell in the human body, our DNA contains our genetic blue print. In the strands of our DNA lie our genes and they determine what we look like.
Peter:
So there are locations in your DNA that influence the way that you look. And each of these genes are playing around with different features of your face and will determine your nose, your eyes.. How everything is set into the face
V/O:
Dr Peter Claes is an engineer and biological imaging specialist at the University Hospital in the Belgium town of Lueven. His current research is focused on one question:
Peter:
Can we deduct facial information from DNA?
V/O:
From very early on Peter had an interest in forensic work and he did his PhD in medical imaging computing, using computer technology to reconstruct faces from skulls to help the authorities with victim identification.
Peter:
I am trying to do as we call computation of biology so using the computer to study biological phenomena. And to unravel relationships that we see in biology. And using these relationships to predict one from the other. If I give you the skull van you predict me the face?
LINK
Facial reconstruction is a very important part of criminal investigations and used all over the world.
V/O:
This is mainly used for victim identification.

In addition, representations of the facial features of criminals are also an important aspect in solving crimes.

However, Lobo das Neves a law enforcement specialist, says that traditional identikits based on what victims can remember are notoriously unreliable.
Lobo:
When a person is involved in a criminal offence, at most times they are under stress. That impedes their memory and certain abilities to describe an event or a description of someone accurately.
Devi:
How reliable are those identikits?
Lobo:
They are as reliable as the co-operation and information between the sketch artist and the witness can be and it is subjective.
V/O:
But although traditional identikits are not very accurate, it is the best we have available.

At the time Peter had no interest in this and continued to work on victim identification.
LINK:
His career took a new turn when a colleague at Penn State University in the USA invited him to participate in a project where a person’s facial features are linked to his or her DNA.
Peter:
Then he contacted me and said: “listen I have a database of people of which I have collected, on the one hand, 3-dimensional images and on the other hand I have also collected DNA samples” he said. And he asked: “Can we deduct facial information from DNA and vice versa.
V/O:
Excited about the large DNA database Peter set to work. DNA not only contains information about gender, but also data about a person’s genetic background and geographical area of origin.
Peter:
For example my genetic background is European. Yours will be a mixture of genetic backgrounds including African. So basically when you can measure genetic background on the level of the DNA the question again is can we relate his background to facial morphologies.
V/O:
The answer was yes. Peter was able to construct basic facial features for a wide variety of populations. He called these base faces. The base faces have the general common characteristics of a specific geographical group.
Peter:
And it is not just restricted Europe, African. Now we can construct base faces for many populations across the world. Asian, Middle-Eastern, Mexican and so forth. And even mixture if you have a combination of different backgrounds.
LINK:
So far Peter has compiled a data base of 32 groups and has identified the base faces for each group.
V/O:
These are base faces of European, Asian and African females. But they are very generic, not distinct and represent features many people in a particular population group share.
Peter:
On top of that we need more information. And that information is actually stored in individual genes in your DNA’s. For example, there is a gene that we have modelled and it is called LRP6 and this gene is influencing the shape of your lips.
V/O:
Scientists working on this specific gene have discovered that individuals have a slightly different codes present on the gene.
Peter:
So depending on the code that you have on this particular gene, your lips are more round, full, sticking out like Pamela Anderson.
V/O:
Or they might be quite thin and straight.
LINK
And so there are literally hundreds of genes that have been identified so far. They code for eye or hair colour, for the shape and size of noses, cheekbones and foreheads and how they are placed.
V/O:
Starting with the data of 20 genes involved in facial morphology, Peter has developed a sophisticated computer algorithm that predicts what a face will look like based solely on DNA data.

He first illustrated this a few years ago using a journalist’s DNA.
Peter:
And we were given a saliva sample from this journalist from which we could tie the full genome from which we could select the gene information that we have been investigating and we predicted her face from her saliva, basically.
V/O:
These are photographs of the journalist and this is the face Peter reconstructed from the DNA in the saliva. The resemblance is startling.

And these are two of his colleagues. The top image is a photograph and the bottom one the likeness the DNA yielded.

The potential for using this technology to help to identify perpetrators of crimes, is obvious, especially since Peter now utilizes the data of 200 genes in his models.
Devi:
DNA has really revolutionized investigations, didn't it?
Lobo:
It surely has. It’s the biggest single crime assistance tool since the discovery of latent fingerprints
V/O:
But even so, sometimes even DNA found on a crime scene can actually be useless.
Lobo:
If you collect DNA from a crime scene and the DNA that you’ve collected cannot be compared to a known person in the database, then that DNA become practically useless until the identification of the subject.
V/O:
The new developments are set to change the use of DNA that cannot be correlated to existing databases.
Lobo:
Now with this DNA you can now use, needless to say, unuseful evidence and turn it into something that is a big tool in the assistance of identifying the perpetrator. It’s very exciting! I think this is going to be ground-breaking science and a big assistance to law enforcement in many, many ways
LINK
Exciting as it seems, Peter warns that his models can never be perfect because he cannot code for environmental factors.
Peter:
If we make a facial prediction from DNA we will always have inaccuracies because we cannot predict someone's environment from DNA. How did the person grow up. Where di he grow up? What kind of nutrition did he or she receive during childhood? Often people expect a one to one look-alike.We will never be able to create a picture of you as if you are on your birthday party and your cousin is taking a picture of you.
V/O:
But despite its limitations Peter’s models can still provide crucial and unique data about individuals.
Peter:
You can say for example this person’s face has a bigger nose, not average. Or has a stronger lower face than average. Or his forehead is more rendered forward or backwards. And it is that kind of description which is of more value to the police.
Lobo:
Investigators do not always need an exact picture of the suspect. A good description of the suspect i.e. the eyes, the mouth, chin, cheekbones, forehead etc is enough for him to go after the suspect And obviously eliminate those that are not suspects in the matter.
Devi:
If this technology becomes available in South Africa, will you consider using it?
Lobo:
I would definitely! I mean its like me saying I’ll ignore fingerprints. Its an absolute helpful tool in the solving of crimes.
LINK:
And what makes the technology even more exciting is that it can also be used outside the area of forensics.
V/O:
It can also be used in the area of historical identity. If DNA of historical figures can be found, facial reconstructions can be done, and we would know what they really looked like.
Peter:
And then you can start to investigate whether Cleopatra had indeed such a big nose that she was famous for.
V/O:
And recent claims that the Mona Lisa’s remains have been found means we can check Da Vinci’s likeness against the real thing.
Voice:
Peter says that since he started this project, he cannot help scrutinizing the faces of people wherever he goes.
Peter:
If I see a very a-typical face, I always wonder what the underlying genetics must be. Its just fascinating what the variation that we see and what the underlying genetics are that are responsible for this variation. It defines who we are and…ja

metadata.Further information: BUILDING THE FACE OF A CRIMINAL FROM DNA The face of a killer constructed from DNA left at the scene of a crime: it sounds like science fiction. But revealing the face of a criminal based on their genes may be closer than we think. Today scientists are using genetic markers from DNA to build up a picture of an offender's face, a process known as molecular photo fitting. A DNA profile is only useful to detectives if a match can be found on a database. This technology offers the tantalising prospect of generating a face from nothing more than a few cells. Dr Peter Claes, a medical imaging specialist at the University of Leuven is doing exactly this. Along with colleagues in the US, he's built up a database of faces and DNA. And armed with this information, he's able to model how a face is constructed based on just 20 genes. Dr Claes believes it contains a lot of information that would be useful to detectives: "I can tell you that your eyebrows are sticking forward more, and your chin as well," he explains. "You have a very prominent specific chin compared to an average European, which in my eyes is not a bad result. You do tend to have flat cheeks, but of course that's a tricky area to actually predict accurately because it's heavily based on diet, which is an environmental factor." At the moment, police couldn't publish a molecular photo-fit like this and hope to catch a killer. But that's not how Dr Claes sees the technique being used in a criminal investigation. "If I were to bring this result to an investigator, I wouldn't necessarily give him the image to broadcast. I would talk to him and say okay, you're looking for a woman, with a very specific chin and eyebrow structure. "So if you're having suspects or candidates that you're looking for, just focus on those." This may be new science, but Dr Claes and his colleagues are rapidly developing the technology. The number of genes used is being expanded from 20 to 200, and is seems clear that molecular photo-fitting is only going to become extremely accurate in the coming years. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ SCIENTISTS RECONSTRUCT FACES FROM DNA SAMPLES Sometime in the future, technicians will go over the scene of the crime. They’ll uncover some DNA evidence and take it to the lab. And when the cops need to get a picture of the suspect, they won’t have to ask eyewitnesses to give descriptions to a sketch artist – they’ll just ask the technicians to get a mugshot from the DNA. That, at least, is the potential of new research being published today in PLOS Genetics. In that paper, a team of scientists describe how they were able to produce crude 3D models of faces extrapolated from a person’s DNA. “We show that facial variation with regard to sex, ancestry, and genes can be systematically studied with our methods, allowing us to lay the foundation for predictive modeling of faces,” the researchers wrote in their paper. “Such predictive modeling could be forensically useful; for example, DNA left at crime scenes could be tested and faces predicted in order to help to narrow the pool of potential suspects.” To arrive at their facial reconstructions from DNA, the researchers looked at the genes that seem to correlate with facial structures, the facial structures of the people with those genes, and then asked people outside of their research group to characterize facial structures along different axes. All of these factors were then used to develop statistical models to approximate a facial structure from DNA. Of course, the process at this point is far from perfect, and there are plenty of obstacles in the way. This study is only for a limited set of genes and populations, and of course, there are many other factors that go into what a face looks like beyond mere genes, such as age and weight. As the researchers note in the paper, “much more work is needed before we can know how many genes will be required to estimate the shape of a face in some useful way and many more populations need to be studied before we can know how generalizable the results are.” Still, they add, “these results provide both the impetus and analytical framework for these studies.” Which means that until it is shown that there is a general way to reconstruct faces from DNA (and it may turn out that there isn’t), cops will still have to find suspects in old-fashioned ways. But if this research pans out, it will provide one more tool that law enforcement can use to accurately determine who might have committed a crime.
